newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Rescuers move bulldozers into Venezuela quake zone.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers move bulldozers into Venezuela quake zone.

text.p: Rescuers switched off listening devices and oxygen feeds late on Friday, leaving bulldozers to clear the rubble left by a quake that devastated eastern Venezuela and killed at least 69, many of them children.
Although the prospect of pulling more people out alive from the flattened buildings appeared slim, hopeful relatives waited nearby and rescue workers promised not to give up.

"Let's hope there are (survivors). But there is very little chance," said fireman Jose Munoz as he supervised work on what was once a six-floor building in the Sucre state capital Cumana, 255 miles (410 km) east of Caracas.
The quake, measured at 6.9 on the Richter scale, struck on Wednesday afternoon, tumbling houses and tower blocks and burying children in their classrooms.
Munoz said oxygen hoses pumping oxygen into the mangled innards of the building had been switched off after special listening devices failed to pick up any traces of life.
Amid the rumble of tractors and beating of jack hammers a small group of relatives huddled together in a tent close by.
Seven people, including 5-year-old twins and their 16-year-old baby-sitter, are believed to be buried inside the ruins from which 23 corpses and more than a dozen survivors have been recovered.
"I know they're alive, I can feel it," said Omar Barrios, father of the twins. "I'm just waiting for them to be rescued."

State Governor Ramon Martinez said 488 people were injured in the quake -- Venezuela's worst for three decades -- and 48 people were pulled alive from wrecked buildings. About 700 buildings were damaged, he said.
The death toll was expected to rise as more bodies were uncovered.
The majority of the deaths occurred in the small agricultural town Cariaco, 40 miles (64 km) east of Cumana, where a high school and nursery school fell on pupils and teachers.
At least 41 bodies were recovered from among the fallen masonry and scattered exercise books. Two-year-old infants and an 81-year-old man were among the dead.

One of the dead, teacher Madeleine de Sanchez, used her large body to protect two of her pupils, locals said. Rescuers found the two girls, still alive, huddled under the 39-year-old teacher's brick battered body.
Cariaco, a town of 13,000, bore the brunt of the quake, which devastated three quarters of its buildings.
Two bodies were uncovered in the ruins of a bakery and another in what remained of the town's pool hall.

Residents on Friday sifted for belongings in the debris of their mud-walled, straw-roofed homes which crumpled the instant the quake hit. Others cooked soups and stews on gas stoves in the cracked, rubble strewn streets.
The town's tiny hospital was evacuated on Thursday due to fears it too might collapse, leaving the injured to be tended in improvised tents.

The dead were buried hurriedly and privately, "because nearly all the corpses were swollen and foul-smelling," said voluntary grave digger Pablo as he stood next to cracked grave stones in the small graveyard.
The French embassy confirmed one French citizen was killed by the quake. There were no other reports of foreigners among the dead or injured.
Government ministers met in emergency session in Caracas on Friday to approve an initial budget of $15 million to repair the infrastructural damage.
The quake, the worst to hit Venezuela since 1967, struck at 3:25 p.m. EDT (1925 GMT) on Wednesday. The epicentre was about 30 miles (49 km) off the northeastern Caribbean coast.
More than 30 aftershocks have been recorded, causing considerable alarm but no further damage.
The 1967 quake killed about 300 in the Venezuela capital and surrounding areas.
